claims.text: Overall tribo-corrosion degradation in high-entropy alloys is governed by the dynamic balance between mechanical removal and corrosion-driven reformation of a passivating oxide film.
Rapid replacement of the oxide removed by sliding enables resistance to coupled degradation.
Failure to reform the oxide rapidly causes localized substrate exposure that accelerates wear and corrosion synergistically.
A polished equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi alloy possesses a native, thin passivating oxide layer formed from its alloying elements.
Simultaneous sliding in 3.5% NaCl can impose coupled mechanical and chemical degradation.
An oxygen supply supports reoxidation of the worn surface.
Enrichment of a passive film in Cr or Al promotes corrosion resistance.
Passive-film thickness, continuity, and reformation kinetics mediate protection against wear and localized corrosion.
Sliding periodically removes the passive layer and exposes fresh metal.
The corrosive environment simultaneously drives reoxidation of exposed metal.
Faster passive-film recovery limits substrate exposure and thereby reduces both wear damage and corrosion-pit development.
An alloy composition or surface treatment that promotes faster protective-oxide reformation will produce less overall degradation than an unmodified equiatomic baseline.
The faster-reforming alloy will exhibit lower wear volume than the baseline.
The faster-reforming alloy will exhibit lower corrosion-pit density and propagation within wear tracks than the baseline.
The prediction should hold when oxygen is available and the load is below that causing bulk failure or disruption of film reformation.
At low oxygen availability or excessive mechanical stress, mechanisms other than passive-film removal and reformation may dominate degradation.
A controlled comparison should test an unmodified baseline and a Cr-enriched surface under otherwise identical tribo-corrosion conditions.
Failure of the modified alloy to show statistically significant reductions in both wear volume and corrosion-pit density would falsify the proposed governing mechanism.
